Affiliation:: Department of Psychology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
Techniques Used: Hierarchical linear regression and moderation analyses
Probing of interactions with simple slopes/prototypical plots
Open-ended content coding and thematic analysis
Fisher’s r-to-z tests for comparing correlation magnitudes
Experimental manipulations with random assignment (appearance- and activity-based prototypicality)
Parametric tornado wind-field modeling and wind-field conditioning (interdisciplinary)
Forensic data integration and wind/structural load-path analysis
preregistration (Study design in transgender health study)
Data & Platforms: Paper 1: N = 131 students (7th–8th grade) from a rural Midwestern middle school; cross-sectional, grade-standardized peer status measures; hierarchical regressions

Paper 2: N = 335 transgender/nonbinary young adults; mixed-methods; data collected via Qualtrics; recruitment via Prolific; scales include MSPSS (family, offline, online), Rosenberg Self-Esteem, GBS, Pride (Testa et al., 2015), Diener Life Satisfaction, WHO-5, UCLA Loneliness, BDI, STAI, and internalized transphobia; qualitative open-ended responses analyzed thematically

Paper 3: Interdisciplinary post-tornado protocol; Fulcrum data platform; on-site data capture with smartphones/360 cameras; wind-field conditioning using a parametric tornado model (Rhee & Lombardo 2018); 117 survivor interviews across nine tornado events; uses wind/structural data collaboration

Paper 4: Open-ended descriptions from 218 undergraduates; content coding into 11 categories across four targets (HS males/females, college males/females); reliability metrics include Cohen’s kappa and Cronbach’s alpha

Paper 5: Two experimental studies with undergraduate samples (Study 1 N ≈ 328; Study 2 N ≈ 249); online surveys presenting photographs or vignettes; within-subjects 2×2×2 designs; analyses via ANOVA/MANOVA
Application Areas: Resilience and mental health in transgender and nonbinary populations
Social support processes across family, offline, and online contexts
Disaster response, sheltering behavior, and load-path understanding
Interdisciplinary methodology bridging psychology with engineering/disaster science
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Integration of multiple perspectives (psychology, education, LGBTQ+ health, disaster science) to address complex social phenomena
Rigorous examination of gender-related processes across development and contexts (adolescence to emerging adulthood; offline vs online environments; appearance vs behavior paradigms)
Emphasis on both predictive relationships (regression, moderation) and descriptive/qualitative insights (interviews, open-ended coding) to triangulate findings
Attention to ecological validity and real-world relevance (rural school context, transgender health, tornado shelters, urban monitoring) and cross-context generalizability
Commitment to methodological transparency, including preregistration and detailed reporting of analytic steps
Summary Description: Dr. Lara Mayeux is a psychologist at the University of Oklahoma whose research spans adolescent development, gender norms, LGBTQ+ health, and interdisciplinary approaches to social resilience. Across her work, she investigates how gender prototypicality and peer/status dynamics operate in adolescence and emerging adulthood, how various social support contexts (family, offline and online friends) relate to positive and negative adjustment for transgender and nonbinary individuals, and how interdisciplinary data streams can inform safety and resilience in disaster contexts. Her methodological repertoire combines robust quantitative analyses (regressions, interactions, ANOVAs, moderation) with qualitative methods (open-ended coding and thematic analysis), and increasingly integrates cross-disciplinary data (wind engineering, forensic analysis, and survivor narratives) to generate theory-driven, actionable insights across settings—from rural middle schools to tornado-impacted communities and beyond.
